⚠ The booklet prints "Answer (3*)" for the radius-of-gyration ratio (solid sphere : hollow sphere). The publisher's own solution (2023_E5 q032) says "* None of the option is correct (correct answer is sqrt(3/5))". The true ratio is sqrt(3):sqrt(5); the starred option (3), 3:5, is its square, so the square roots were lost from the printed options. Same question as 2023_F1 q001.

stepsRecall the moment of inertia of a solid sphere about a diameter, 25MR2 → Recall the moment of inertia of a thin hollow sphere about a diameter, 23MR2 → Use k = I/M for each and form the ratio solid : hollow, in that order
confusing options2 of 4 · options 3, 4

In hydrogen spectrum, the shortest wavelength in the Balmer series is λ. The shortest wavelength in the Bracket series is
  1. 9λ
  2. 16λ
  3. 2λ
  4. 4λ
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. The shortest wavelength of a series is its series limit, n2 → ∞, so 1λmin = Rn12.
  2. Balmer (n1 = 2): 1λ = R4, so λ = 4R.
  3. Brackett (n1 = 4): 1λ' = R16, so λ' = 16R.
  4. λ'λ = 164 = 4, so λ' = 4λ, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultymedium · 2 steps
stepsRecognise that the shortest wavelength of a series is its series limit (n_upper -> infinity), so 1/λ = R/n2 and λ is proportional to n2 of the lower level → Use n = 2 for Balmer and n = 4 for Brackett and take the ratio (42)/(22) to express the Brackett limit in terms of λ
confusing options2 of 4 · options 2, 4
16 λ is exactly what a candidate gets by writing λ proportional to n2 for Brackett and forgetting to divide by Balmer's own factor of 4 (treating λ as R-limit 1/R), while 4 λ is the properly taken ratio; 9 λ (Paschen-style n=3) and 2 λ (unsquared n ratio) are weaker slips a prepared candidate rarely lands on.
why it is trickyMedium: two short steps once the series limit is recognised, but option 2 (16 λ) is a real rival that sits exactly on the lost-normalisation slip, so only correctly taking the ratio n_B2/n_Ba2 separates it from option 4; options 1 and 3 fall away on sight.
the catchThe live rival 16 lambda is the result of using n^2 = 16 directly instead of the ratio 16/4, a classic lost-factor error inside a known method; the candidate must also know Brackett's lower level is n = 4 and that 'shortest wavelength' means the series limit.

Two bodies of mass m and 9m are placed at a distance R. The gravitational potential on the line joining the bodies where the gravitational field equals zero, will be (G = gravitational constant)
  1. -16GmR
  2. -20GmR
  3. -8GmR
  4. -12GmR
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. At the null point a distance x from m: Gmx2 = G(9m)(R-x)2.
  2. Taking square roots: R - x = 3x, so x = R4.
  3. Distance from 9m is R - R4 = 3R4.
  4. V = -GmR/4 - G(9m)3R/4 = -4GmR - 12GmR.
  5. V = -16GmR, which is option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 highagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsSet the field magnitudes equal at the null point between the masses: Gm/x2 = G(9m)/(R-x)2 → Solve for the position: R-x = 3x, so x = R/4 from m and 3R/4 from 9m → Add the two scalar potentials at that point: -Gm/(R/4) - 9Gm/(3R/4) and simplify
confusing options2 of 4 · options 1, 4
Option 4 is exactly the 9m term alone (-12Gm/R), what a candidate gets by forgetting the contribution of the smaller mass, so it sits right beside the full sum; options 2 and 3 do not come from any obvious slip.
why it is trickyMedium: three short steps on a standard null-point pattern, and only one real rival -- option 4 is the potential of the 9m body alone, so a candidate has to remember to add both terms, while options 2 and 3 fall away once the null point at R/4 is found.
the catchPotential is a scalar sum of both bodies even though the fields cancel there; dropping the smaller mass's -4Gm/R term lands exactly on option 4.

READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
If the galvanometer G does not show any deflection in the circuit shown, the value of R is given by
  1. 100 Ω
  2. 400 Ω
  3. 200 Ω
  4. 50 Ω
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. With no deflection in G, no current flows through the 2 V branch, so the potential difference across R equals 2 V.
  2. The 10 V cell then drives current only through 400 Ω and R in series: I = 10400 + R.
  3. VR = IR = 10R400 + R = 2.
  4. 10R = 800 + 2R ⇒ 8R = 800 ⇒ R = 100 Ω, which is option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 highagree
difficultymedium · 2 steps
stepsRecognise that zero galvanometer current means the potential across R (the node between R and G) equals the 2 V cell's emf, so the 2 V branch carries no current → Treat 400 ohm and R as a series divider on the 10 V cell: 10R/(400+R) = 2, i.e. 8 V across 400 ohm gives the current, and solve for R
confusing options1 of 4 · option 1
No option is the exact product of a standard slip -- inverting the divider ratio gives 1600 ohm and including the 2 V cell as a source in the loop gives values not offered -- so once the 2 V-across-R condition is set up only one option survives, and 400, 200 and 50 ohm are just round-number fillers of the same magnitude.
why it is trickyMedium: two short steps whose first is a small but essential insight (no deflection means R sits at exactly 2 V and the right-hand branch is dead); the options, all in the same hundred-ohm range, do not let a candidate skip that insight, but once it is made the divider settles it with no rival to separate.
the catchThe null-deflection condition must be translated into 'potential across R = 2 V'; a candidate who instead writes a two-loop Kirchhoff analysis with the galvanometer branch carrying current spends extra time, though no option rewards that route.

stepsJudge Assertion A: in ΔrG = -nFEcell, Ecell is fixed for the reaction, so ΔrG scales with n, the number of electrons in the reaction as written. R is true → Decide whether R explains A: does the intensive/extensive distinction account for why ΔrG carries the factor n, i.e. why doubling the balanced equation doubles ΔrG but leaves Ecell unchanged

the catchBoth statements are true, so the whole question rests on the explanation link. Whether intensive/extensive explains the n-dependence is a conceptual call, and a candidate who sees two independent true facts lands on option 4.

solver reasoning: E_cell is intensive and Delta_rG is extensive, so Delta_rG = -nFE_cell scales with n (moles of electrons); R explains why A holds.

Consider the following compounds/species:
[Figure: structures i–vii]
The number of compounds/species which obey Huckel’s rule is ______.
  1. 2
  2. 5
  3. 4
  4. 6
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)

no worked solution is printed for this question

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. i. Naphthalene: planar, cyclic, conjugated with 10 π electrons = 4(2)+2, so it obeys Huckel's rule.
  2. ii. Cyclopentadienyl anion: 4 π electrons from two C=C plus the lone pair gives 6 π electrons = 4(1)+2, so it obeys.
  3. iii. Cyclobutadiene: 4 π electrons = 4n with n=1, antiaromatic, does not obey.
  4. iv. Cyclopropenyl anion: 2 π from C=C plus the lone pair gives 4 π electrons = 4n, does not obey.
  5. v. Cyclopropenyl cation: 2 π electrons = 4(0)+2, so it obeys.
  6. vi. Cyclooctatetraene: 8 π electrons = 4n and tub-shaped (non-planar), does not obey.
  7. vii. Anthracene: 14 π electrons = 4(3)+2, so it obeys.
  8. Species obeying: i, ii, v, vii, so the count is 4, which is option 3.

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · medium
  1. Dehydration is easiest when the H removed is acidic and the alkene formed is stabilised by conjugation.
  2. In option 1, CH3-CH(NO2)-CH(OH)-CH2OH, the H on C3 is α to -NO2 and therefore acidic.
  3. Loss of H2O across C2-C3 gives CH3-C(NO2)=CH-CH2OH, in which the C=C is conjugated with -NO2.
  4. In options 2 and 3 the OH carbon is not next to the NO2-bearing carbon, so no conjugated nitroalkene forms; option 4 has no activating group.
  5. Hence option 1 is dehydrated most readily.

difficultyhard · 3 steps
stepsRead each structure from the figure and locate the OH relative to the NO2-bearing carbon in each (options 1-4 are drawn only in the crop; the text options are blank but the question image carries them). → Decide which mechanism governs acid dehydration here: plain carbocation (E1) stability, which the electron-withdrawing NO2 destabilises when near, versus the acidity of the H on the carbon carrying NO2 and the conjugated nitroalkene the elimination can form. → Compare the candidates on that basis (OH β to C-NO2 in 1 and 3, OH remote from NO2 in 2, no NO2 at all in the 1,3-diol 4) and pick the most readily dehydrated one.

why it is trickyHard: only three short steps, but the key move is a method choice that is not signposted - the routine E1 carbocation-stability trend points to option 2, while the α-H acidity / conjugation argument points to the NO2-adjacent alcohols 1 and 3, which then must be separated from each other, so three options stay live.
the catchOrganic reaction-condition insight: the candidate must abandon the standard 'more stable carbocation dehydrates faster' rule in favour of the nitro group's effect on the neighbouring C-H and the conjugated product; the rule-following answer is a live rival, and the options are drawn as skeletal structures that must be decoded first.

solver reasoning: In 3-nitrobutane-1,2-diol the C2-OH has an H on the adjacent C3 that is made acidic by the -NO2 group, so loss of water gives a conjugated nitroalkene (C=C-NO2), the most stabilised product.

On balancing the given redox reaction,
aCr2O72- + bSO32-(aq) + cH+(aq) → 2aCr3+(aq) + bSO42-(aq) + c2H2O(l)
the coefficients a, b and c are found to be, respectively-

The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)

Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
  1. Oxidation states: Cr in Cr2O72- is +6, in Cr3+ is +3; S in SO32- is +4, in SO42- is +6.
  2. Electrons gained per Cr2O72-: 2 × 3 = 6; electrons lost per SO32-: 2.
  3. Equate electrons: 6a = 2b ⇒ b = 3a; take a = 1, b = 3.
  4. Charge balance: left -2 - 6 + c, right 2(+3) + 3(-2) = 0, so c - 8 = 0 ⇒ c = 8.
  5. Check oxygen: left 7 + 9 = 16, right 12 + c2 = 12 + 4 = 16. Balanced.
  6. a, b, c = 1, 3, 8, which is option 3.

why it is trickyHard: after B removes options 1 and 2 the question comes down to two live options separated only by a single altered word in statement A ('fascicle' for 'fascia'), and statement D is also an altered line (M line for the Z-line boundary of a sarcomere), so the candidate has to check four statements and catch two NCERT-line alterations.
the catchStatement A is NCERT's sentence with one word changed: fascicle (the bundle) and fascia (the connective tissue layer) appear side by side in the same NCERT line, so a candidate who recognises the sentence without reading the keyword picks option 3.

stepsRecall the NCERT list of mammalian features: hair, external ear (pinna), mammary glands, dicondylic skull, direct development → Check each option's three features and eliminate any option containing a feature not unique to mammals (indirect development, monocondylic skull, tympanic membrane)
confusing options2 of 4 · options 3, 4
Option 3 swaps pinna for tympanic membrane, an altered NCERT line that tempts a candidate who knows mammals have ears but forgets that frogs, reptiles and birds also have a tympanum, so the word 'unique' is what rules it out.
why it is trickyMedium: each option is the same triplet with one word changed, and options 1 (indirect development) and 2 (monocondylic skull) fall to a prepared candidate on sight, but option 3 survives unless the candidate reads 'unique' and remembers that the tympanic membrane is shared with other vertebrates.
the catchThe keyword 'unique': tympanic membrane is a real ear structure present in mammals but not unique to them, so the altered-line option 3 is a live rival to the pinna option.
